This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 263 columns across 11 data files.
#### Issues Identified

10 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 11 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. **The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. text.text: Structural equation modeling (SEM) is often used to evaluate theories about how psychological constructs relate to one another.
In practice, researchers frequently compare SEMs with criteria such as BIC because they are fast and widely available.

However, these shortcuts hide the assumptions behind the comparison and make it hard to incorporate prior knowledge-for example, that certain effects should be small, or that they should be positive rather than negative.
This paper presents a practical workflow that makes Bayes factor model comparison feasible for typical SEMs while keeping these assumptions transparent.

The workflow starts from a baseline that mirrors what BIC implicitly assumes, and then shows how conclusions change when researchers incorporate reasonable alternative prior knowledge that reflects theoretical expectations.
We also extend our workflow to robust mixture priors to make evidence assessment less dependent on a single prior choice.
Our workflow also helps when a model consists of multiple competing structural explanations.

Instead of selecting a single "best" model and treating it as certain, we demonstrate Bayesian model averaging, which combines results across models (and across priors) to reflect uncertainty about which relations are truly present and how large they are.
The overall goal is to make evidence for structural hypotheses easier to compute, easier to scrutinize, and easier to communicate.
Structural equation modeling (SEM) offers a flexible framework for inference on latent variables and their relationships.
A standard inference task in this field involves model comparison, where possibly non-nested, structurally different models are pitted against one another.
In applied Bayesian SEM, model evaluation and comparison can be approached in different ways.

One popular approach focuses on posterior predictive checks and predictive criteria such as leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO; Gelman et al., 2014; Vehtari et al., 2017) and the Watanabe-Akaike information criterion (WAIC; Depaoli, 2021; Depaoli et al., 2023; Watanabe, 2010).
text.formatted: One popular approach focuses on posterior predictive checks and predictive criteria such as leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO; <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Gelman et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Vehtari et al., 2017)</ref> and the Watanabe-Akaike information criterion (WAIC; <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Depaoli, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Depaoli et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Watanabe, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: These tools are informative for diagnosing model misfit and model misspecification; moreover, these tools are comparatively prior-insensitive in that their conclusions do not depend strongly on the prior distributions that are assigned to the model parameters.

At the same time, these tools leave unaddressed a key goal, which is to quantify relative evidence for competing structural hypotheses: LOO and WAIC estimate how well a fitted model will predict new data, so differences in the estimates are read as differences in predictive accuracy, not as the relative likelihood of either model.

More specifically, LOO and WAIC are unable to provide strong support for a simpler model even when it is true and sample size is large (e.g., Gronau and Wagenmakers, 2019a; for a discussion, see Gronau and Wagenmakers, 2019b; Vehtari et al., 2019).

text.text: To quantify relative evidence, we focus on marginal likelihoods, that is, the probability of the observed data under a model after averaging over the model's parameter prior.

Marginal likelihoods provide a common currency for Bayesian model comparison in SEM: ratios of marginal likelihoods yield Bayes factors for pairwise comparisons (e.g., Jeffreys, 1935; Jeffreys, 1961), and when combined with prior model probabilities they yield posterior model probabilities.

text.text: This paper is structured as follows.
We approximate BIC's implicit unit-information prior by an explicit prior and use bridge sampling to estimate marginal likelihoods, providing a baseline for prior-sensitivity analyses.

Building on this baseline, we introduce a limited number of UI-prior variants that encode modest substantive knowledge about focal structural relations, with the goal of obtaining a sharper and more appropriate measure of evidence.

These variants illustrate how modest substantive assumptions about the structural relations can sharpen model comparison while keeping the likelihood and structural model specification fixed.

The first extension concerns robust mixture priors for which we blend a weakly informative unit-information component with an informative component that encodes directional and variational expectations about focal structural relations.

text.text: The second extension concerns Bayesian model averaging (BMA) across a large set of structural candidate models.

Rather than having all inference rest on a single selected model, Bayesian model averaging propagates model uncertainty by weighting each model's contribution by its posterior model probability (Hoeting et al., 1999; Jeffreys, 1961; Kaplan & Lee, 2016; Madigan & Raftery, 1994a; Wrinch & Jeffreys, 1921).

text.text: To establish a computational baseline that is closely connected to BIC-type Bayes factors, we construct explicit unit-information (UI) priors by using information from maximum likelihood (ML) fits.

This baseline serves two functions: it approximates the BIC's implicit prior assumptions by an explicit prior, and it provides a controlled reference point for assessing the impact of incorporating additional prior information in later sections.

text.text: The double use of the data is concentrated in the UI baseline, which borrows both location (MLE centering) and scale from the data; the zero-centered variants introduced below remove the data-dependent centering for the focal parameters and retain only the data-dependent dispersion, that we regard as relatively diffuse.

Because blavaan by default expresses prior distributions through a set of univariate families, we implement the unit-information (UI) baseline in a parameter-wise way: each free parameter is assigned a univariate prior whose mean and variance match its UI targets, and the joint prior is taken as the product across parameters.

Consequently, we do not attempt to reproduce the full UI prior covariance structure implied by the ML sampling covariance matrix; instead, the UI construction is implemented parameterwise to capture the intended "one-observation" informativeness for each free parameter.

This strategy mirrors a simplified unit-information construction proposed by Ntzoufras (2009), who replaces the multivariate UI prior by independent priors with means equal to the posterior means under a flat (improper) prior and with variances equal to the corresponding posterior variances multiplied by N , yielding a convenient BIC-like baseline for model comparison.

text.text: The blavaan package provides a convenient set of priors tailored to common SEM parameter types, such that the distributional form is naturally matched to the parameter block: normal priors for loadings and regressions, gamma priors for variance-type parameters, and beta priors (after transformation) for correlations.

Therefore we assign priors by parameter block (corresponding to free elements of Λ, B, Θ, and Ψ) and determine the associated hyperparameters by moment matching so that each prior attains its unit-information mean and variance targets.
This yields a UI-prior baseline for the prior-sensitivity analyses and extensions considered in later sections.

For each free factor loading λ and structural regression coefficient β (i.e., free elements of Λ and B), we use a normal prior, where µ j equals either the ML estimate θj (UI-centering) or 0 in the zero-centered variants described below, and Var UI (θ j ) = N Var( θj ).

For variance-type parameters v j > 0 (free diagonal elements of Θ and, where applicable, Ψ), we assign a gamma prior to the variance itself (the [var] option in blavaan; the blavaan default is a gamma prior on the standard-deviation scale), with (a j , b j ) chosen by moment matching so that the prior mean equals the ML estimate vj and the prior variance equals the unit-information target N Var(v j ).

text.text: The latent variances (the diagonal of Ψ) are free parameters only in the simulation study, where the latent variables are identified by marker variables; in all other analyses the latent variables are identified by fixing their variances.
For the latent variances we additionally bound the shape a j below at 0.5 while keeping the prior mean, because the unit-information approach can otherwise place most of the prior mass near zero.

For each focal latent correlation ρ ∈ (-1, 1), we place a beta prior on the transformed parameter x = (ρ + 1)/2 ∈ (0, 1), where (a, b) are selected by matching the desired mean and unit-information variance of ρ (equivalently, of x).
In some cases, the UI-implied variance would correspond to a beta distribution with extreme or ill-behaved shape parameters.
In those cases, we apply mild regularization in two steps.
First, we re-express the beta parameters in terms of an "effective prior sample size" n 0 via a = xn 0 and b = (1 -x)n 0 (so that a+b = n 0 ).

We then (i) cap n 0 at a moderate value (here n0 ≤ 10) to avoid excessively concentrated priors, and (ii) enforce unimodality by requiring a ≥ 1 and b ≥ 1, implemented by imposing a lower bound on n 0 that guarantees both inequalities given the target mean x.
After applying these bounds, we set a and b from the bounded n 0 , which preserves the intended mean and yields a dispersion close to the UI target while ensuring a numerically stable beta prior.
In practice, we have found that our regularization for the extreme cases often leads to a uniform distribution, that is, Beta(1, 1).

Because correlation matrices must be positive definite, the prior that blavaan samples need not coincide with the specified beta prior; in our analyses this affects only the datacentered UI baseline, not the zero-centered variants introduced below (see Appendix A.2).
In the present paper, we use blavaan with Stan to leverage Stan's efficient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling while retaining the convenience and reproducibility of standard SEM syntax.

Our UI construction is therefore designed to operate within this fast Stan-based workflow: we translate unit-information targets into the prior families supported by blavaan/Stan and calibrate their hyperparameters by moment matching.
This preserves the practical advantages of the blavaan-Stan pipeline while still yielding a unit-information baseline for the prior-sensitivity analyses that follow.

text.text: Let M e denote the unconstrained (encompassing) model and M c the corresponding constrained model.

The constrained model M c is obtained by restricting the parameter space of M e to values that satisfy C. M c has the same likelihood as M e , but uses the encompassing prior truncated to C and renormalized.
Let p(y | M e ) denote the marginal likelihood of the encompassing model under the chosen prior.

The marginal likelihood of the constrained model M c can be obtained via the encompassing-prior approach as where Pr(C | M e ) is the prior probability mass that the encompassing prior assigns to the constrained region C, i.e., the integral of the encompassing prior over C; and Pr(C | y, M e ) is the corresponding posterior probability mass under the encompassing model.
In practice, we apply this adjustment on the log scale for numerical stability.

In the implementation, Pr(C | M e ) is estimated by MCMC draws from the joint prior distribution using blavaan's prior sampling option (prisamp=TRUE), and Pr(C | y, M e ) is estimated from posterior MCMC draws as the proportion of draws satisfying the constraints.

Concretely, we fit the unconstrained model M e under the chosen prior, obtain prior draws from the same model, compute the prior and posterior constraint probabilities as proportions of draws satisfying C. In our applications, M e corresponds to the unconstrained version of the structural model M 1 ; hence the constrained comparison against M 0 is obtained by replacing p(y | M 1 ) with p(y | M c ) in the Bayes factor.

Because the adjustment multiplies the marginal likelihood of the encompassing model, the twosided Bayes factor under the same prior is always available alongside the directional one; we recommend reporting both, so that it is transparent how much of the evidence stems from the directional restriction.

We estimate Pr(C | M e ) using blavaan's prior sampling option rather than by evaluating the constraint probability analytically or by sampling from separate univariate priors, because the constraints C are defined on the joint distribution of the focal parameters under the full SEM parameterization.

Even when the user specifies seemingly independent priors on individual parameters, the effective prior on the model-implied latent covariance matrix is shaped by identification constraints, in particular the requirement of positive definiteness (for details, see Merkle et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Even when the user specifies seemingly independent priors on individual parameters, the effective prior on the model-implied latent covariance matrix is shaped by identification constraints, in particular the requirement of positive definiteness (for details, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Merkle et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Prior sampling via blavaan therefore yields a direct Monte Carlo estimate of Pr(C | M e ) under exactly the same parameterization, transformations, and constraints used for posterior sampling and bridge sampling.
With this MCMC-based sampling strategy it is important to monitor how often the constrained region is visited.
If only a tiny fraction of prior or posterior draws satisfy C, the Monte Carlo estimates of Pr(C | M e ) and/or Pr(C | y, M e ) can be unstable.

Substantively, very small Pr(C | M e ) indicates that the encompassing prior assigns little mass to the hypothesized direction, suggesting a mismatch between the directional claim and the chosen prior parameterization; very small Pr(C | y, M e ) indicates that the data place little posterior mass in the constrained region.

In either case, the first remedy is typically to reconsider the directional specification (e.g., by shifting or concentrating prior mass toward the theoretically expected region), rather than merely increasing the number of draws.

When the constrained region genuinely has very low probability but is still of interest, it can help to use estimators that are designed for inequality constraints rather than relying on the raw "fraction-of-draws" count.

For example, Sarafoglou et al. (2023) provide a practical workflow for order-restricted hypotheses that replaces brute-force counting by a more efficient Monte Carlo strategy tailored to the constrained region.

text.text: Another pragmatic alternative is to replace the raw proportion estimator by the result of fitting a parametric distribution to the prior and posterior draws (e.g., a multivariate normal on an unconstrained scale, or a copula-based model) and then estimating Pr(C | M e ) and Pr(C | y, M e ) under the fitted density.

In our extensions, if no draw satisfies the constraint, we do not treat the estimated probability as exactly zero; we use the rule-of-three upper bound (Hanley & Lippman-Hand, 1983; Jovanovic & Levy, 1997), 3/ESS, where ESS is the effective number of draws, and report the resulting Bayes factor as a bound.

text.text: Regardless of the computational tactic that is employed, inspecting these probabilities remains useful because it reveals the extent to which the directional constraint is aligned with the prior and with the data.

Our simulation study serves three purposes.
First, it provides a fully controlled setting in which the data-generating model is known, allowing us to illustrate the complete priorto-Bayes-factor workflow.

Second, it demonstrates how incorporating modest substantive information-here, simple directional expectations on focal structural relations-can improve model selection relative to a purely unit-information (BIC-like) baseline, which may otherwise favor overly simple structural specifications when the true model is comparatively complex.

Third, because informative priors can also mislead, it examines their cost: we cross three data-generating conditions (M 1 true, M 1 true with halved focal effects, and M 0 true) with three sample sizes, so that the behavior of the priors can be assessed when the focal effects are weak or absent and not only when they are present.

text.text: In the second step, we also report a "wrong-direction" variant (UI-0-dir (wrong)) in which the directional constraint is intentionally set opposite to the data-generating signs (i.e., it requires the focal regressions and the latent covariance to be negative).

This condition is included purely as a sanity check: if the method behaves as intended, imposing a direction that contradicts the data-generating process should yield overwhelming evidence against the directional hypothesis, thereby illustrating how directional Bayes factors appropriately penalize substantively implausible (or misspecified) sign restrictions.
Firstly, the results confirm that the bridge-sampled log Bayes factors under the UI-type priors closely track the log Bayes factors as obtained from the BIC approximation.

text.text: At the same time, the bridge-sampled UI log Bayes factors tend to be slightly larger than their BIC counterparts, as reflected by the mild upward displacement of the point cloud relative to the equality line.

This small disparity is expected: the BIC Bayes factor relies on a large-N Laplace approximation under a specific implicit unit-information prior, whereas bridge sampling evaluates the marginal likelihood under the exact UI prior used in our fits.

Because our UI prior is implemented as a product of univariate, block-specific priors, it is generally not identical to the multivariate normal unit-information prior that is implicit in the standard BIC/Laplace derivation.

One reason is the prior on the bounded latent residual correlation: a Beta prior cannot be as dispersed as the unit-information variance of this parameter requires (in our implementation its shape parameters are bounded below by one, so it is at most uniform), which makes it more concentrated than the corresponding normal prior and can therefore raise the log marginal likelihood of M 1 .

Overall, these results highlight a common problem: when the data are only moderately informative, default large-sample approximations such as BIC (and closely related unitinformation baselines) may yield Bayes factors that are comparatively weak and therefore less decisive for selecting among substantively distinct structural models.

Moreover, because the BIC penalty grows with the number of free parameters, it can be especially conservative in complex settings such as SEM, where comparatively rich models are easily penalized even when they capture genuine (but moderately large) effects.

In contrast, modest and theory-consistent prior refinements can substantially sharpen the comparison. 4In our simulation, reducing the dispersion of the focal priors (UI-0-half) increases the frequency of strong evidence for the data-generating model, and incorporating directional expectations (UI-0-dir) strengthens the evidence further when the imposed direction is correct.

We use this proxy Depression dataset for two applied demonstrations.
First, we show how robust mixture priors can be implemented in Bayesian SEM within our UI-type prior construction framework.

Second, we use the same dataset to illustrate Bayesian model averaging (BMA) over a set of competing structural specifications: we evaluate candidate models using bridge sampling (after pruning the model space), and then perform BMA to address model selection uncertainty in a principled manner.

The first component, π 1 , is a vague baseline prior for these focal relations: we use the UI-0 specification (zero-centered unit-information priors on the focal regressions) together with blavaan defaults for nonfocal parameters.

The second component, π 2 , is a more informative directional prior: it combines (i) reduced prior standard deviation for the focal relations (UI-0-half) with (ii) positivity constraints imposed via the encompassing-prior approach (UI-0-dir), yielding a UI-0-half-dir specification.

Concretely, we evaluate the directional component by treating the UI-0-half prior as an encompassing prior and applying the standard adjustment based on prior and posterior mass in C, with C denoting the set of order constraints on the focal parameters (e.g., all focal effects are positive; see Subsection "UI-0-dir" for details).
This mixture specification guards against undue sensitivity to a single informative directional prior.
In our application we use an equal-weight mixture (w = 0.5), so that the evidence reflects a balanced compromise between a vague baseline and theoretical expectations.

More generally, the weights encode the analyst's confidence in the directional expectation: the more confident the analyst is about the sign, the more weight 1 -w is placed on the directional component π 2 , and moderate confidence corresponds to an intermediate weight such as w = 0.5.

Intuitively, when posterior mass concentrates in the region emphasized by the directional half-variance prior, the marginal likelihood increases; when the theoretical expectations are not supported, the vague baseline component limits the penalty from potentially misspecified directionality.
In this way, the mixture yields a comparison that is informative about the presence of the effects while remaining conservative with respect to their assumed direction.
When the analyst has greater prior confidence in the expected direction and scale of the focal relations, the weight on the informative prior component may be increased accordingly.

Bayesian model averaging (BMA) addresses a pervasive challenge in SEM: even when the measurement model is held fixed, the structural part induces an extremely large model space because many paths can be fixed or freed independently, often leaving the data compatible with a range of rival specifications rather than a single dominant one.

In such settings, the common two-step workflow-first selecting a 'best-fitting' model and then conditioning all inference on that selection-creates model myopia: uncertainty from the selection stage is discarded, which can yield overly confident conclusions about which structural relations are present and about their estimated magnitude (e.g., Hoeting et al., 1999; MacCallum & Austin, 2000; Madigan & Raftery, 1994b; Wagenmakers et al., 2021 Wagenmakers et al., , 2022)).

text.text: Let {M k } K k=1 denote a set of K candidate structural models that share the same measurement model but differ in which focal structural relations are freely estimated versus fixed to zero.
Given marginal likelihoods p(y | M k ) and prior model probabilities p(M k ), the posterior model probabilities are determined by
Standard Bayesian model averaging (BMA) combines inference across these models by averaging a quantity of interest ∆ with respect to the posterior model probabilities.
However, the marginal likelihoods-and consequently the weights p(M k | y)-depend on the specific choice of prior distributions for the model parameters.
To prevent substantive conclusions from being contingent on a single prior specification, we extend the averaging framework to include uncertainty regarding the prior itself.
Let {π s } S s=1 denote a set of plausible prior specifications (e.g., varying in dispersion or directionality), each assigned a prior probability p(π s ).
In the present application we set S = 4 and consider four focal-prior variants, all of them with blavaan default priors on the non-focal parameters.

First, UI-0 serves as a baseline that encodes little information about the focal structural relations beyond symmetry around zero (i.e., it does not favor either direction and retains a relatively diffuse unit-information dispersion).
Second, UI-0-half is a more informative variant that reflects the expectation that effects are unlikely to be large.
Third, UI-0-dir incorporates directional information by imposing positivity constraints on the focal relations via the encompassing-prior approach under the UI-0 specification.
Fourth, UI-0-half-dir combines both restrictions by imposing the same positivity constraints under the UI-0-half specification (i.e., with reduced focal prior variance).

The 'grand' posterior distribution of ∆ is then obtained by averaging over both the structural models and the prior settings: where p(M k , π s | y) is the joint posterior probability of model M k and prior specification π s .
This formulation results in a comprehensive mixture distribution that propagates uncertainty from both the structural specification and the prior shape into the inference stage.

In realistic SEM settings, the number of candidate models K can be very large because each candidate structural relation may be either included or fixed to zero, resulting in an exponential growth of the model set.
For the model in Figure 2, there are m = 10 candidate structural relations, yielding K = 2 m = 1024 structural submodels.

text.text: In many applications, theory can be used to restrict attention to a smaller, substantively motivated subset of models, but such preselection risks overlooking plausible alternatives.

Rather than committing to a hand-picked subset, we use a two-stage strategy: a fast BIC-based Occam-window screening step to identify a small set of high-support candidates (Kaplan & Lee, 2016; Madigan & Raftery, 1994b), followed by fully Bayesian refitting of the selected candidates to obtain posterior model probabilities via bridge-sampled marginal likelihoods.

text.text: We apply our analysis procedure to the same Depression proxy dataset that was introduced earlier.

We first fit the fully specified structural model by maximum likelihood in lavaan using factor-variance identification (std.lv=TRUE) and screen the downward space of nested submodels using a BIC-based search.

We traverse the tree of submodels obtained by fixing candidate latent regressions and covariances to zero, and we expand a model (i.e., evaluate its descendants) only if its BIC lies within an Occam window of the best BIC encountered so far.

Following Kaplan and Lee (2016) we set C = 20, so models are expanded only when ∆BIC ≤ 2 log(20) ≈ 6 relative to the current best model; under the BIC approximation, this corresponds to excluding models that are worse than roughly 20 : 1 in Bayes-factor terms compared to the current best model.

text.text: Models outside this window are not expanded, and their descendants are not explored.
To assess the impact of this screening rule, we also exhaustively fit the full model space (which is feasible here; 210 = 1024 models).
We found the highest-ranked models to be identical across the screened and exhaustive search.
When the window constant C is chosen to be relatively lenient, this set can still be larger than is practical for full Bayesian refitting.

We therefore add a second screening phase, in which the BIC values from the models that survived the first screening phase are used to compute approximate posterior model probabilities under a uniform model prior; we then retain the smallest subset whose cumulative approximate posterior mass reaches 99%.

This second screening step acts as a simple size control: it keeps the Bayesian refitting stage focused on a small number of high-support candidates (often only a handful) while discarding models that collectively carry negligible BIC-implied weight.

We then refit each retained model in blavaan under each of the four prior settings (UI-0, UI-0-half, UI-0-dir, UI-0-half-dir, with blavaan default priors on the non-focal parameters), using four MCMC chains with 1,000 warmup iterations and 4,000 post-warmup iterations per chain.

Marginal likelihoods are estimated via warp-III bridge sampling in the bridgesampling R package, and posterior model probabilities are computed from these marginal likelihoods assuming equal prior probabilities over the retained models.

On the same computer as in Extension I, the BIC-based screen evaluated 187 of the 1,024 possible models in about 15 seconds, and the Bayesian refits of the five retained models took about 30 minutes in total (roughly 6 minutes per model: two bridge-sampled fits, which took 2.4 minutes on average and 5.2 at most, and two prior-sampling runs of about half a minute each); the complete analysis took about 36 minutes.
To obtain the final prior-averaged BMA summaries, we assign equal prior weights to the four prior settings and compute posterior weights as proportional to p(y | M k , π s ) p(M k ) p(π s ).

Model-averaged posterior parameter distributions are then formed as a mixture over (k, s): for symmetric priors, we use posterior draws directly from the fitted models; for the directional setting, we retain only draws satisfying the inequality constraints (rejection sampling from the encompassing posterior).
Parameters fixed to zero in a given model contribute a point mass at zero.
This produces grand-mixture posterior summaries that jointly reflect structural and prior uncertainty.

The BIC is a common and convenient tool for model selection in structural equation modeling.
Its popularity is understandable: it is available by default in SEM software, cheap to compute, and provides a simple penalty-based trade-off between fit and complexity.
At the same time, BIC is only an asymptotic approximation to Bayesian model comparison.

In particular, its Bayes-factor interpretation rests on a specific, implicit unit-information parameter prior that is effectively fixed by the approximation: researchers do not have a practical way to modify this prior to reflect substantive knowledge (e.g., plausible effect sizes, or directional expectations about focal paths).
Moreover, the BIC-Bayes-factor link is accurate only up to an O(1) prior-dependent constant that can matter in finite samples.

As a consequence, BIC-based conclusions can be sensitive to sample size and can understate model uncertainty, especially in SEM settings where models can be complex, sample sizes can be modest, and signals may be weak.

The goal of this paper was to make marginal-likelihood-based evidence measures (i.e., Bayes factors and posterior model probabilities) practical and transparent for SEM users, while retaining the flexibility to incorporate substantive prior information about latent relations.
We pursued this goal in three steps.
First, we constructed an explicit unitinformation (UI) prior from maximum-likelihood fits and estimated marginal likelihoods via bridge sampling.
This "UI baseline" approximates BIC's prior assumptions by an explicit prior and provides a controlled reference point for sensitivity analyses.

Second, we showed how the UI baseline can be sharpened by incorporating modest substantive prior information about focal structural relations, both by reducing the prior scale (UI-0-half) and by imposing directional expectations via an encompassing-prior adjustment (UI-0-dir), yielding more decisive evidence when these assumptions are appropriate.
Third, we illustrated how these tools naturally extend to applied workflows: robust mixture priors and Bayesian model averaging (BMA) across a large set of structural submodels.
Across the simulation and extensions, two messages emerge.

The first is methodological: bridge sampling combined with blavaan provides a broadly applicable route to marginal likelihoods for SEMs specified in standard syntax, so that Bayes factors become available without bespoke Stan coding; moreover, this workflow is not tied to UI-type priors and can be used with any proper prior supported by blavaan, including weakly informative and substantively elicited specifications.
The second is substantive: prior specification matters for marginal-likelihood-based comparisons, but this sensitivity can be made informative rather than problematic.

By explicitly stating and varying priors for focal relations-rather than relying on an implicit default-researchers can assess robustness, encode expectations when warranted, and quantify how much such assumptions sharpen or weaken the inferences.

In the BMA setting, this same machinery yields posterior inclusion probabilities and model-averaged parameter summaries that propagate structural uncertainty instead of conditioning on a single selected model.
LOO, WAIC, and posterior predictive checks, discussed in the Introduction, complement Bayes factors in this workflow.
Because a Bayes factor is conditional on the candidate model set, it cannot show that all candidate models fit poorly.

A natural workflow is therefore to assess model adequacy first, for instance with posterior predictive checks or the landscape analysis used in Extension I (Appendix A.3), and then to use Bayes factors to compare the models that adequately describe the data.

Although our simulation focused on nested comparisons, the workflow is not restricted to them: bridge sampling estimates each model's marginal likelihood separately, so Bayes factors for non-nested models are obtained in the same way.

What changes is the correspondence with BIC, which is better behaved for nested models (Kass & Wasserman, 1995); for non-nested comparisons we expect it to be looser, which strengthens the case for estimating marginal likelihoods directly.

Zero-centering, dispersion-halving, and directional constraints can be applied to the structural relations within each model about which the analyst holds the corresponding expectation, and should be applied symmetrically across models unless genuinely asymmetric substantive knowledge warrants otherwise.
The unit-information construction helps here, because it calibrates each prior to one observation's worth of information and thereby places both models on a common, data-calibrated scale.
For applied use, computing cost is modest.

An analysis requires only a handful of fits, each of which takes a few minutes on a standard computer when the chains run in parallel (Extensions I and II took about 10 and 36 minutes in total); the fits are independent and can be parallelized further, and the posterior sample size can be reduced when the bridge-sampling error is small.
The number of candidate models grows exponentially with the number of candidate structural paths, which is why a screening step restricts Bayesian refitting to a small set of high-support models.

For substantially larger models, fitting time and memory, which grow with the number of indicators, free parameters, and posterior sample size, rather than the stability of the bridge-sampling estimate, are the practical constraints.
Three limitations are worth noting.

First, although the encompassing-prior approach offers a practical solution for directional hypotheses in software that does not support truncation directly, it requires stable estimation of constraint probabilities and may become computationally inefficient when the constrained region has very small prior or posterior mass; in such cases, more specialized estimators for order-constrained hypotheses may be preferable (e.g., Sarafoglou et al., 2023).

text.text: Second, full model-space exploration remains computationally challenging for large SEMs; our screening strategy uses BIC only as a pragmatic pruning device, after which final inference is fully Bayesian.
Because the screen is based on BIC, it does not take the targeted priors into account, so a discarded model could in principle be favored by them.

As a rough guide, relative to its value under the zero-centered unit-information prior (UI-0), a targeted prior can raise a model's marginal likelihood by a factor of at most about 4 k for k focal parameters (2 k from correct directional constraints and 2 k from halving the focal prior scale), so models somewhat outside the window cannot be ruled out.
This is only a heuristic, and does not provide guarantees.

In larger model spaces, where exhaustive checking is infeasible, screening based on the target priors themselves, for example Savage-Dickey density ratios computed from a single fit of the full model under multivariate-normal or Gaussian-copula approximations, may be preferable.
Fast approximate Bayesian methods such as the INLAvaan package (Jamil & Rue, 2026) may make such screens practical, which we leave to future research; we have not evaluated them here.

text.text: In settings where theory strongly restricts the candidate set, researchers may prefer to define a smaller set of substantively motivated models and apply the same bridge-sampling and BMA tools to that curated model space.
Third, no simulation can cover every condition.
Ours used one SEM structure, standardized loadings fixed at 0.7, and normally distributed indicators, so the results need not carry over to other structures, weaker measurement, or nonnormal data.
In particular, nonnormality that leaves the covariance structure unchanged is invisible both to the normal-likelihood workflow and to the covariance-based landscape analysis (Appendix A.3).

Overall, the workflow developed here (Figure 1) aims to bring Bayesian evidence measures closer to routine SEM practice: (i) start from a baseline connected to BIC, (ii) introduce targeted and interpretable prior information for focal structural relations, (iii) compute marginal likelihoods via bridge sampling, and (iv) propagate model uncertainty through posterior model probabilities and BMA when many candidates are plausible.

text.text: When blavaan switches from beta to LKJ at the block level, it sets the LKJ shape parameter using the first beta prior it encounters for a parameter in that correlation matrix.

For example, if the first encountered prior is Beta(4, 1), blavaan assigns LKJ(4) to the corresponding block; if the first encountered prior is Beta(1, 1), it assigns LKJ(1), which is uniform over correlation matrices.
For a single correlation, that is, a 2 × 2 block, LKJ(a) is the symmetric Beta(a, a) on (-1, 1).
This behavior implies that a correlation-specific beta prior may not be applied literally when the relevant correlations are part of an unrestricted block.
Figure A.1 illustrates this behavior.

We placed an informative Beta(4, 1) prior, which concentrates mass near ρ = +1 (prior mean 0.6), on each of the three correlations among three latent variables, so that they form an unrestricted 3 × 3 block, and we sampled the joint prior with the prior-sampling option of blavaan (prisamp = TRUE).

The sampled marginals are symmetric about zero (means of 0.00) and bear little resemblance to the specified density: the beta priors were replaced by an LKJ(4) prior on the block, which discards the specified location.
Such a prior, which places most of its mass on high correlations, is also poorly suited to sampling.
Further details on how blavaan handles correlation-matrix priors and positive-definiteness constraints are described in Merkle et al. (2023).

Concretely, latent covariances enter our analyses as a focal parameter in the simulation, as non-focal parameters with blavaan's default prior in Extension I (where the focal parameters are regressions), and as candidate paths in the model-averaging analysis.

text.text: We fit each model to the data by maximum likelihood and generate datasets from each fitted model's implied covariance matrix by parametric bootstrap.
Each generated dataset is scored by its BIC-approximated log marginal likelihood under both models, which gives one cloud of points per model in the plane of the two log marginal likelihoods.
The observed data are then located in this plane.
Data inside the clouds are reproduced by the models; data far outside both clouds are not, whatever Bayes factor they yield.

text.text: In SEMs with free latent (residual) correlations, prior specification must respect the requirement that the implied correlation matrix is positive definite.

Assigning independent beta priors to individual correlations is convenient and interpretable, but such marginal specifications need not correspond to any coherent joint prior over a correlation matrix.
In particular, independently sampled correlations can violate positive definiteness, especially when multiple correlations are free within the same block.

To address this, recent versions of blavaan may replace beta priors on individual free correlations with an LKJ (Lewandowski-Kurowicka-Joe) prior on any unrestricted correlation-matrix block (Lewandowski et al., 2009).
